quiz.q: What does git commit actually do?
options: Records the staged changes as a snapshot in local history
quiz.explain: A commit is a local snapshot of the staging area. Uploading happens later with git push.

quiz.q: Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?
options: Git is version control software; GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tools
They are two names for the same product
Git can only be used with GitHub
quiz.explain: Git runs locally and works offline. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform built around Git.

quiz.q: Which command sets the email attached to your commits for every repository?
quiz.explain: git config --global writes to your user-level config, so the value applies to all repositories.

quiz.q: What is the staging area for?
options: Choosing exactly which changes go into the next commit
Storing backups of your repository on GitHub
Keeping a list of deleted branches
Temporarily hiding files from your editor
quiz.explain: Staging lets you assemble a commit from selected changes, even within the same file.

quiz.q: Which command shows changes that are not staged yet?
quiz.explain: git diff compares the working directory with the staging area. Add --staged to compare staging with the last commit.

quiz.q: Which command stages all changes, including brand-new files?
quiz.explain: git add -A stages modifications, deletions, and untracked files. git add -u only stages tracked files.

quiz.q: You add build/ to .gitignore, but build output is still tracked. What happens?
options: Nothing changes until you remove the files from the index with git rm --cached
Git deletes the folder from disk
Git stops tracking the files immediately
quiz.explain: .gitignore only affects untracked files. Already-tracked files must be removed from the index.

quiz.q: When is git commit --amend safe?
options: On a local commit that nobody else has pulled
On any commit, as long as you push afterwards
quiz.explain: Amending rewrites the commit hash. Doing it on shared history forces everyone else to clean up.

quiz.q: What is a Git branch, technically?
options: A movable pointer to a commit
A full copy of the project folder
quiz.explain: Branches are tiny: a name pointing at a commit. That is why creating one is instant.

quiz.q: Which command creates a branch and switches to it immediately?
quiz.explain: git switch -c creates and checks out the new branch in one step. git branch alone only creates it.

quiz.q: When can a merge be a fast-forward?
options: When the target branch has not moved since the feature branch started
Only when both branches have new commits
When the branches have conflicting files
quiz.explain: A fast-forward simply slides the target pointer forward. If both sides moved, Git needs a three-way merge.

quiz.q: In a conflict, what does the ======= line separate?
options: Your current branch's version and the incoming branch's version
The commit message from the diff
quiz.explain: Everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is yours; between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming side.

quiz.q: What does git remote add origin <url> do?
options: Stores a URL under the name origin; nothing is uploaded yet
Clones the repository into the current folder
quiz.explain: A remote is a named bookmark for a URL. You still need git push to send commits.

quiz.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: pull fetches and then integrates into your branch; fetch only downloads
quiz.explain: fetch updates remote-tracking branches safely. pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase).

quiz.q: Which credential does GitHub accept for HTTPS Git operations?
quiz.explain: Password authentication for Git was removed. Use a fine-grained or classic personal access token, or switch to SSH.

quiz.q: What does the -u flag in git push -u origin main do?
options: Sets the upstream so later pushes and pulls know the destination
quiz.explain: -u sets tracking between your local branch and the remote branch, so plain git push and git pull work afterwards.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a fork and a branch?
options: A fork is a copy of the whole repository under your account; a branch lives inside one repository
A fork is local; a branch is on GitHub
A branch can only be created from a fork
quiz.explain: Forking copies the repository to your account so you can push without permission on the original.

quiz.q: In the fork workflow, which remote do you push your feature branch to?
options: origin, which points at your fork
upstream, which points at the original project
You push directly to the original repository
quiz.explain: You push to your fork (origin), then open a pull request from your branch to the original repository.

quiz.q: What does writing Closes #42 in a pull request description do?
options: Closes issue 42 automatically when the pull request merges
Blocks the merge until issue 42 is closed manually
quiz.explain: GitHub links the PR to the issue and closes it on merge into the default branch.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid committing directly to main in a fork?
options: It makes syncing with upstream and keeping pull requests clean much harder
GitHub deletes forks that commit to main
Git does not allow commits on main
It automatically closes all your pull requests
quiz.explain: Keeping main as a clean mirror of upstream lets you fast-forward it and keeps each PR limited to its own branch.

quiz.q: Which command discards unstaged edits to one file?
quiz.explain: git restore rewrites the working file from the index. The change is lost, so stash first if unsure.

quiz.q: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do?
options: Removes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
Deletes the last commit and all its changes
Creates a new commit that undoes the last one
Moves the changes to a stash
quiz.explain: Soft reset moves the branch pointer only. The changes remain staged, ready to recommit.

quiz.q: Which command is safe for undoing a commit that is already on a shared branch?
quiz.explain: Revert adds a new inverse commit, so nobody else's history is rewritten.

quiz.q: What can the reflog recover?
options: Commits that existed locally, even after a reset or branch deletion
Uncommitted edits discarded with git restore
Deleted files that were never committed
quiz.explain: The reflog records HEAD movements. Uncommitted work was never in a commit, so it cannot be recovered this way.

quiz.q: What does rebasing a branch do?
options: Replays its commits on top of another branch, creating new commit hashes
Merges another branch with a merge commit
quiz.explain: Rebase rewrites the branch's commits onto a new base, producing a linear history with new hashes.

quiz.q: What is the golden rule of rebasing?
options: Do not rebase commits that other people have already pulled
Always rebase main before every commit
quiz.explain: Rebasing replaces commits. If others have them, their history diverges from yours.

quiz.q: When is cherry-pick the right tool?
options: Copying a specific fix onto a release branch
Squashing all commits on a branch
quiz.explain: Cherry-pick copies selected commits. For whole features, merge or rebase instead.

quiz.q: What makes an annotated tag different from a lightweight tag?
options: It stores a message, author, and date
It can only be created on GitHub
quiz.explain: Annotated tags are full Git objects with metadata, which is why releases should use them.

quiz.q: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live?
quiz.explain: GitHub reads YAML workflow files from .github/workflows in the repository.

quiz.q: What can GitHub Pages host?
options: Static files such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Any server-side application with a database
Private repositories on the free plan
quiz.explain: Pages serves static content only. Backend logic must live elsewhere.

quiz.q: How private is a secret gist?
options: Unlisted but readable by anyone with the link
Encrypted and visible only to you
quiz.explain: Secret gists are hidden from search but not access-controlled. Never store credentials in them.

quiz.q: You accidentally pushed an API token. What is the first thing to do?
options: Revoke and rotate the token immediately
Delete the file in a new commit
quiz.explain: Assume the token is already compromised. Rotate it first, then clean history if needed.
